page.title: Portable Solar Panel with Charge Controller: Which Kit Fits Your Battery (2026)
page.h1: Portable solar panel with charge controller: match the kit to what you charge
page.desc: A suitcase panel's built-in controller is for a 12 V battery. We compare ACOPOWER, Renogy, VEVOR and BLUETTI kits on LiFePO4 support, controller limits and price.
page.answer: Short answer. A portable solar panel with a built-in charge controller is for charging a bare 12 V battery; a power station bypasses it. Pick ACOPOWER's 100W ProteusX suitcase ($189): LiFePO4 preset, 20A controller rated to 360 W. Renogy's 100W/200W Voyager needs lithium voltage set by hand.

What the differences mean

  • Cost per rated watt: ACOPOWER ProteusX $189 ÷ 100 W = $1.89/W; ACOPOWER PLK 120W $259.99 ÷ 120 W = $2.17/W; Renogy 100W $229.99 ÷ 100 W = $2.30/W. VEVOR works out to $129.90 ÷ 200 W = $0.65/W, but VEVOR's page doesn't list the battery types its controller supports.
  • Price gap at 100 W: the Renogy 100W kit costs $229.99 − $189 = $40.99 more than ACOPOWER's ProteusX, and its lithium setting is manual.
  • Controller headroom: ACOPOWER rates its 20A controller at 20 A × 18 V = 360 W on a 12 V system. 360 W ÷ 100 W = 3.6× the ProteusX panel, so ACOPOWER's add-on to 200 W stays inside the limit.
  • Real output: OutdoorGearLab measured an average of 49.7 W in direct sun from Renogy's 100 W foldable suitcase. 49.7 ÷ 100 = about half the label rating, so plan on roughly 50 W from a 100 W suitcase.
  • MPPT upgrade: ACOPOWER's PTK 200W kit has a 20A MPPT controller for $399, which is $399 − $189 = $210 more than the ProteusX. ACOPOWER claims 10–20% more output than PWM. That figure is the maker's claim, not a measurement.

The built-in controller only serves a 12 V battery

A suitcase controller sits between the panel and a bare battery. It sets the charge stages and stops overcharging. ACOPOWER says its included controller "must be used to charge 12V batteries". For a power station it says to "use the solar panel connector cables provided and plug them into the cables that came with your power station". Its page also says a 12 V battery and a power station can charge at the same time. BLUETTI says the same thing from the station side: "your BLUETTI station already manages the solar optimization", so no separate controller is needed.

Renogy's suitcase uses the Voyager 20A PWM. Renogy lists it for Gel, AGM and Flooded batteries with a "Lithium option", and adds: "For lithium batteries, it is essential to manually set the voltage." ACOPOWER's 20A controllers list LiFePO4 among eight presets. On an older Renogy suitcase, The Camping Nerd had to add MC4 connectors between the panel and the Voyager before it could charge a Goal Zero Yeti, and the author notes that the change voids the warranty.

The "20A" on these controllers is a limit on the current into the battery, not extra power. It caps how much panel you can add (360 W at 12 V for ACOPOWER) but doesn't raise what the panel produces. If you mainly want to charge a power station, a kit like {buy:bluetti-elite-30-v2-100w-solar-kit} avoids paying for a controller you'd bypass.

Not recommended

VEVOR 200W with 30A PWM, for a LiFePO4 battery. It is the cheapest 200 W option at $129.90. But VEVOR's page names no battery types for its controller, and the panel weighs 26.23 lb net. A lithium owner can't confirm a LiFePO4 charge profile before buying. ACOPOWER's ProteusX lists one for $189.
